title: Truth
hookLine: Pilate asks what truth is and walks out; the Dominicans made the word their motto

lines: A GOVERNOR, A PRISONER, EARLY MORNING.
HE DOESN'T WAIT FOR THE ANSWER.
cards: A Roman governor, early in the morning, in his own headquarters. A prisoner stands before him, hands tied, and says he came into the world to give testimony to the truth.
The governor, Pilate, answers with a question people still ask at kitchen tables and in philosophy classes. In the Douay-Rheims: "What is truth?" Then John's Gospel adds a detail that's easy to miss.
Pilate doesn't wait. He goes straight back out to the crowd. A question that large, and he walks out on it.
Today, an order that decided to stay in the room. Its motto is one word: truth.

teach.b: The word is veritas, Latin for truth, and the Dominicans carry it as their motto, on their crests and over their schools.

teach.h: QUID EST VERITAS? EST VIR QUI ADEST.
teach.b: In the Latin Bible a medieval friar read, Pilate's question is quid est veritas, what is truth. Someone later noticed a word game: rearrange the letters and you get est vir qui adest, it is the man who is here.
The answer was standing in front of Pilate the whole time. That's the Christian claim under the motto. In John's Gospel, Jesus says, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life."
So for a Dominican, truth isn't only a set of correct statements.
It's someone to follow. And it isn't meant to stay private. Jesus promises in John that "the truth shall make you free."
Free, not cornered. That shapes how the truth gets told. Paul's letter to the Ephesians has a phrase for it: "doing the truth in charity."

Truth without charity becomes a weapon; charity without truth becomes flattery. The order's own history shows how hard it is to keep the two together, and in a few days this path will look at that honestly.

teach.h: THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.
teach.b: But the motto still points at a simple daily task: say what is real, as someone who wants the other person to be free.

how: Veritas appears on the shields and in the mottos of Dominican houses, schools and colleges; Dominicans connect it to study, preaching and the belief that Christ is the truth.

s: in John's Gospel, Pilate waits to hear the answer to 'what is truth?'
he asks, and goes straight back outside to the crowd.
quid est veritas can be rearranged into est vir qui adest
'what is truth?' becomes 'it is the man who is here.'
in Ephesians, truth is paired with charity
'doing the truth in charity': truth told for the other person's good.

games.q: you're Pilate. you've just asked the prisoner, 'what is truth?' what do you do next?
o: wait and listen to his answer.
go back outside to the crowd.
games.why: John's Gospel says he went straight back out. the question gets asked, and the answer, Christians say, was standing right there.

practice: Bring to mind one true thing you've been avoiding saying to someone, a worry about a friend, that you were hurt, that you were wrong, and just find the sentence, without saying it yet.

Turn it over slowly, the way you'd want to hear it if you were them, taking out the sharp edge and keeping the truth; if you pray, ask for courage and gentleness together, and if not, sit with the sentence until it feels both honest and kind.

wordCard.voice: Veritas. Latin for truth, and the Dominican motto: truth that is someone to follow, and truth told in charity. Today's word.
